summary: A guide, published as an FYI, that explains to newcomers how the IETF works and what to expect when attending a meeting. It was replaced by RFC 1718.

eli5.summary: A welcome guide for a new student at a big school, telling how clubs work, where to go, and what the unwritten rules are.

how do i attend an ietf meeting
how do i prepare for an ietf meeting
subtitle: A newcomer's guide to understanding the IETF and attending its meetings.

tldr.problem: New attendees at IETF meetings face confusion about the organization's structure, how meetings work, and what to expect.
tldr.mechanism: This guide explains the IETF's mission, history, hierarchical structure, meeting logistics, how to prepare, and where to find resources. It covers everything from dress code to where to find RFCs.
tldr.outcome: New IETF attendees understand how the organization works and can participate effectively. RFC 1718 supersedes this version with updates.

today: RFC 1539 is an Informational FYI document that has been superseded by RFC 1718, which includes updates reflecting changes in the IETF structure and meeting logistics from 1993 to 1994.

sections.title: What is the IETF
sections.content:
The Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) is a loosely self-organized group of engineers and researchers who contribute to the engineering and evolution of the Internet and its technologies. It is the principal body developing new Internet standard specifications. Its mission includes identifying and proposing solutions to pressing Internet problems, specifying protocols and near-term architecture, making recommendations to the IESG about standardization, facilitating technology transfer from the IRTF, and providing a forum for information exchange between vendors, users, researchers, and network managers.

Importantly, the IETF is not a traditional standards organization and has no official membership. Anyone may register and attend meetings. The closest equivalent to membership is being on IETF or working group mailing lists, where the best information about current activities can be found. The IETF meets three times a year.
sections.eli5: The IETF is a group of volunteers who meet three times a year to improve the Internet. It is not a company or official club—anyone can attend. The real work happens through mailing lists and meetings where people discuss and decide on new Internet technologies.

sections.title: Organization and Hierarchy
sections.content:
The IETF sits within a larger organizational structure. The Internet Society (ISOC) is the professional society overseeing Internet growth and standardization. The Internet Activities Board (IAB) is a technical advisory group chartered to oversee Internet architecture and protocol design. The Internet Engineering Steering Group (IESG) manages IETF activities and the standards process. The IETF divides into nine functional areas: Applications, Internet Services, Network Management, Operational Requirements, Routing, Security, Service Applications, Transport, and User Services. Each area has at least one Area Director.

Below the areas are Working Groups, where actual technical work happens. Each Working Group operates under a charter to achieve specific goals. Birds of a Feather (BOF) sessions are informal meetings, usually held once or twice, to gauge interest in forming a new Working Group. Working Group members are people on that group's mailing list, though anyone may attend meetings.
sections.eli5: The IETF is organized like a company with management layers. The Internet Society is at the top. Below that are committees (IAB and IESG) that make decisions. The IETF splits into nine teams, each led by a director. Inside each team are working groups of people focused on solving specific problems.

sections.title: Meeting Logistics and Getting Started
sections.content:
To attend an IETF meeting, you must register and pay a fee. Early registration (about one month before) costs less than late registration. Registered attendees receive a packet containing an orientation sheet, an At-A-Glance guide showing room assignments and maps, working group acronyms, and a name tag—this At-A-Glance is essential throughout the week.

Newcomers should attend the Newcomers' Orientation, typically held on Sunday afternoon before the opening plenary. It covers what is in the attendee packets, the meaning of colored dots on name tags (red for IAB, yellow for IESG, blue for Working Group chairs, green for local hosts), and how to read the At-A-Glance. The opening plenary on Monday morning is most heavily attended and provides important introductory remarks, so attendance is encouraged.

The dress code is informal. Many newcomers overdress in suits, only to find everyone else in t-shirts and jeans. The general rule is 'dress for the weather.' An important social tradition is the IETF social event, a non-technical gathering designed for people to meet and relax together.
sections.eli5: To go to an IETF meeting, you sign up and pay a fee. You get a packet with maps and schedules. Newcomers get an orientation to explain how everything works. Dress casually. There is a party where people meet each other socially.

sections.title: Being Prepared and Using Mailing Lists
sections.content:
Preparation is critical for productive attendance. Before the meeting, you should read documents that Working Group and BOF chairs distribute, follow discussions on relevant mailing lists, or review archived messages. The more work done on mailing lists before the meeting, the less time the meeting needs to spend on basic discussion, leaving more time for productive technical work.

To stay informed, join the IETF announcement mailing list (send a request to ietf-announce-request@cnri.reston.va.us), where all meeting information and announcements are posted. You may also join the IETF discussion list (ietf@cnri.reston.va.us) for technical discussions. Do not send subscription requests to the lists themselves—use the '-request' addresses. Most Working Groups have their own mailing lists for discussions specific to their work.

Working Groups typically go through phases: an initial phase where all ideas are welcome, a development phase where a solution is chosen, and a final phase for refinement. Once an issue has been decided, trying to reopen it is considered bad form. The InterNIC archives contain documents that Working Group chairs place before each meeting; these should be reviewed by attendees planning to participate.
sections.eli5: Before attending, read the documents and follow the mailing list so you understand the issues. Use the '-request' address to join lists, never the main list. Working groups move through phases, and you should understand the current phase before suggesting changes.

sections.title: Documentation and Finding Information
sections.content:
RFCs and Internet-Drafts are crucial references. RFCs are formal documents that may specify standards, describe informational topics, or provide operational guidance. The FYI subseries documents overviews and introductory topics, while the STD subseries identifies RFCs that specify Internet standards. If an RFC is revised, it gets a new RFC number, but FYI and STD numbers remain constant for reference.

Internet-Drafts are working documents valid for six months that may be updated, replaced, or obsoleted. They should not be cited as archived materials or standards.

Before an IETF meeting, the InterNIC establishes an archive on ds.internic.net in /pub/current-ietf-docs with documents organized by area and working group. These documents remain for about two months after the meeting. Access is available via anonymous FTP or Gopher. After the meeting, IETF Proceedings are compiled over two months and sent to attendees. They include the final agenda, IESG report, area and working group reports, slides, and an attendee list.
sections.eli5: RFCs are official documents about how Internet protocols work. FYI documents are introductions. Internet-Drafts are papers still being written. Before meetings, working group leaders put important documents in an online archive that you should read. After meetings, the Proceedings are published with all the presentations.
